title: RAG vs Fine-tuning
summary: The single most common confusion in AI product work. One changes what the model can see; the other changes how the model behaves.

a.label: RAG
a.tagline: Changes what the model can access

axes.label: What it changes
axes.a: The context supplied at question time

axes.label: Solves
axes.b: Wrong tone, format, or task-specific skill

axes.label: Failure mode
axes.b: Learned the wrong pattern; hard to undo

axes.label: Who can maintain it
axes.a: Anyone who can update a document
axes.b: An ML engineer with a training pipeline

verdict: Reach for RAG when the model lacks *knowledge*. Reach for fine-tuning when the model lacks *behaviour*. If the honest answer is "it does not know our policies", fine-tuning will not fix it. Try prompt engineering first, RAG second, fine-tuning last.
diagram:
KNOWLEDGE PROBLEM            BEHAVIOUR PROBLEM
  "It does not know            "It knows, but answers
   our refund policy"           in the wrong format"
         |                              |
         v                              v
       RAG                        FINE-TUNING
         |                              |
   retrieve policy doc          train on 500 examples
         |                              |
         v                              v
   grounded answer            consistently formatted
   with a citation                   answer

title: API model vs Local model
summary: Where the weights live decides your cost curve, your latency floor and your entire data-governance story.

axes.label: Quality ceiling
axes.b: Very good, usually a step behind frontier

axes.label: Versioning
axes.a: The vendor may deprecate or change it
axes.b: The file on disk never changes

verdict: Start on an API to find out whether the feature is worth anything. Move to local when privacy, per-token cost at volume, or offline operation forces it. "We must self-host" is a constraint, not a default.
diagram:
API MODEL                       LOCAL MODEL

   your app                        your app
      |                               |
      v  (network)                    v  (localhost)
   vendor endpoint                 Ollama / vLLM
      |                               |
   frontier weights                weights on your disk
      |                               |
      v                               v
   pay per token                   pay for hardware
   data leaves                     data stays

title: Vector DB vs SQL DB
summary: Not competitors. They answer fundamentally different questions, and most real systems run both.

a.label: Vector database
a.tagline: Finds things that mean the same

verdict: A vector database is a search index, not a system of record. Keep the truth in SQL. Keep the meaning in vectors. If someone proposes replacing Postgres with a vector database, something has gone wrong.
diagram:
"How many users churned in March?"  ->  SQL
   "Which docs discuss cancellations?" ->  VECTOR

              PRODUCT
                 |
        +--------+--------+
        |                 |
     SQL DB           VECTOR DB
   system of record   search index
   exact answers      similar answers

title: Keyword search vs Semantic search
summary: Exact tokens versus meaning. Each fails in exactly the place the other succeeds, which is why hybrid search exists.

axes.label: Matches
axes.b: Vectors that point the same way

axes.label: Handles typos
axes.a: Only with fuzzy matching bolted on

axes.label: Explainability
axes.a: Obvious — the word is right there

axes.label: Cost
axes.b: Embedding cost per document and per query

verdict: Hybrid search is usually correct. Run both, then fuse the rankings. Users search for product codes and for concepts in the same session, and a system that only does one will feel broken half the time.
diagram:
QUERY: "how do I cancel"        QUERY: "ERR-4021"

   keyword  -> weak               keyword  -> exact hit
   semantic -> strong             semantic -> noise

              HYBRID SEARCH
                    |
        +-----------+-----------+
        |                       |
   BM25 ranking          vector ranking
        |                       |
        +----------+------------+
                   |
              fuse + rerank
                   |
              final results

title: Agent vs Chatbot
summary: A chatbot answers. An agent decides and acts. The difference is not intelligence — it is whether it has hands.

axes.label: Steps
axes.a: One turn in, one turn out
axes.b: A loop until the goal is met or it gives up

axes.label: Side effects
axes.b: Real — it can write, send, refund, delete

axes.label: Failure cost
axes.b: A bad action in a real system

axes.label: Latency
axes.b: N model calls plus N tool calls

axes.label: Cost
axes.b: Unbounded unless you cap the loop

verdict: The moment a system can take an action, your problem changes from "is the answer good" to "who authorised that, and can we undo it". Ship read-only tools first, write tools behind approval second.
diagram:
CHATBOT                   AGENT

   user                      user
     |                         |
     v                         v
   model                     model --> decide
     |                         |          |
     v                         |       call tool
   answer                      |          |
                               |<---- observe
                               |  (loop, capped)
                               v
                            answer + side effects

title: Prompt engineering vs Context engineering
summary: Prompt engineering is what you say. Context engineering is what you put in the room before you say it.

b.label: Context engineering
b.tagline: Deciding what information is present at all

axes.label: Fails when
axes.b: The right information was never there

axes.label: Typical fix
axes.a: Add an example, tighten the format
axes.b: Retrieve better chunks, drop irrelevant ones

verdict: If the model has the facts and still answers badly, that is a prompt problem. If the facts were never in the window, no amount of prompt polishing will help. Diagnose which one you have before iterating.
diagram:
CONTEXT ENGINEERING            PROMPT ENGINEERING
   (what goes in the window)      (how you ask)

   system prompt        \
   retrieved chunks      \
   conversation history   >---> [ CONTEXT WINDOW ] ---> MODEL
   tool definitions      /              ^
   user question        /               |
                                 the instruction
                                 lives in here too

title: Training vs Inference
summary: Training is when the model learns. Inference is when it answers. They have completely different cost, hardware and risk profiles.

axes.label: Hardware
axes.b: One GPU, or even a CPU

axes.label: Cost driver
axes.a: Total compute for the whole run
axes.b: Tokens per request times request volume

verdict: A model does not learn from your users during inference. If someone believes a conversation "taught" the model something permanent, that is a misconception worth correcting immediately — it has privacy and expectation-setting consequences.
diagram:
TRAINING (once)                INFERENCE (every request)

   huge dataset                   one prompt
        |                              |
        v                              v
   forward pass                   forward pass
        |                              |
   compute loss                   sample next token
        |                              |
   backward pass                  repeat until done
        |                              |
   UPDATE WEIGHTS                 WEIGHTS UNCHANGED

title: Pretraining vs Fine-tuning
summary: Both are training. One builds general capability from scratch; the other nudges an existing model toward a specific behaviour.

axes.label: Data
axes.a: Trillions of tokens of raw text
axes.b: Hundreds to thousands of curated examples

axes.label: Cost
axes.b: Tens to thousands of dollars with LoRA

verdict: You will never pretrain. You may fine-tune. Understanding pretraining matters because it explains the knowledge cutoff, why hallucination happens, and why the model "sounds confident about everything".
diagram:
raw internet text
          |
     PRETRAINING          (months, millions of dollars)
          |
          v
     BASE MODEL           good at continuing text
          |
     INSTRUCTION TUNING   (thousands of examples)
          |
          v
     CHAT MODEL           good at following instructions
          |
     YOUR FINE-TUNE       (hundreds of examples)
          |
          v
     SPECIALISED MODEL

title: Open-source model vs Closed model
summary: Open weights buy you control, portability and inspectability. Closed models buy you capability and someone else operating it.

axes.label: Auditability
axes.a: Weights and often data are inspectable

verdict: "Open source" is often really "open weights" — the training data and code are usually not published. That distinction matters legally. Always read the actual licence rather than the word "open".
diagram:
OPEN WEIGHTS                CLOSED

   download the file           call the endpoint
        |                            |
   run anywhere                 vendor infrastructure
        |                            |
   quantize / fine-tune         use as offered
        |                            |
   you operate it               they operate it
        |                            |
   pinned forever               deprecation notices

title: LLM-as-judge vs Human evaluation
summary: One scales and is cheap but biased. The other is the ground truth but does not scale. You need both, in the right proportion.

axes.label: Known biases
axes.a: Prefers longer answers, its own style, first position

verdict: Never deploy an LLM judge you have not calibrated against humans. Label 100 examples by hand, measure agreement, and only then let the judge run unattended. An uncalibrated judge is a confident number with no meaning.
diagram:
100 HAND-LABELLED EXAMPLES  (the golden set)
              |
              v
       run the LLM judge
              |
       measure agreement  ---- low ----> fix the rubric
              |                              |
            high                             |
              |<-----------------------------+
              v
   judge runs on thousands of cases automatically
              |
   humans spot-check a sample + all disagreements

title: Exact search vs ANN
summary: Exact search compares against everything. Approximate search takes a calculated shortcut — and that trade is the whole reason vector search is viable.

axes.label: Build time
axes.b: Index must be built and rebuilt

verdict: Below roughly 50,000 vectors, exact search is fast enough and has no failure mode. Do not introduce ANN tuning until the collection actually demands it. Premature ANN is a common source of silently missing results.
diagram:
EXACT                        ANN (HNSW)

   query                        query
     |                            |
     v                            v
   compare to ALL              enter graph at top layer
   1,000,000 vectors                |
     |                          hop toward closer nodes
     v                              |
   perfect top-k                    v
   (slow)                      descend layers
                                    |
                                    v
                              near-perfect top-k
                              (fast, ~98% recall)

title: Cloud inference vs Local inference
summary: Same model, different place. The decision is rarely about quality and almost always about data, cost shape and control.

a.label: Cloud inference
a.tagline: Runs in someone else’s data centre

axes.label: Idle cost
axes.b: You pay whether or not it is used

axes.label: Break-even
axes.a: Better at low or spiky volume

verdict: Model the break-even honestly. Local inference wins when volume is high and steady, or when data simply cannot leave. It loses badly on spiky traffic, because you pay for peak capacity around the clock.
diagram:
COST
    ^
    |            cloud (linear in usage)
    |          /
    |        /
    |      /
    |----/------------------- local (flat, after upfront)
    |  /  |
    | /   |
    |/    break-even
    +------------------------> VOLUME

   Below break-even: cloud.  Above and steady: local.
